alt: Orange and blue atmospheric layers above Earth's curved horizon, with a crescent Moon in the black sky.
caption: Earth's atmosphere seen edge-on from the ISS on 6 December 2021. Its coloured bands reveal a thin envelope above the surface.

alt: Crescent-shaped dunes around Lagoa dos Barros on Brazil's Atlantic coast, seen from the ISS.
caption: Wind shapes barchan dunes beside Lagoa dos Barros, Brazil. The crescent tips point downwind.

alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon: living vegetation is a carbon store, exchanging carbon with the air and soil.

alt: Grassland with scattered acacia trees in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania.
caption: Serengeti savanna: seasonal rainfall helps explain the balance between grasses and scattered trees.

alt: Aerial photograph of Spurn Point curving across the Humber estuary entrance.
caption: Spurn Point, England, photographed in 2024. Longshore transport supplies a spit at the Humber estuary.

alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

caption: ASTER, 24 September 2005: tributaries dissect sandstone in Canyonlands, Utah. A drainage network collects flow towards a main river.

caption: NASA ARIA displacement mapping after the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake. Colours encode surface movement, rather than the colour of the ground.

alt: NOAA sea-surface temperature anomaly map with warmer-than-average water across the equatorial Pacific in late 2015.

alt: Tilted and folded sedimentary beds exposed at The Settlands coast.
caption: Folded strata at The Settlands, Wales. Trace a bed through the exposure to see deformation recorded in solid rock.

alt: A low shelf cloud sweeps over buildings at Brock University in Ontario.
caption: A cold front passes Brock University, St. Catharines, Canada. The cloud edge makes uplift visible; the front itself is a zone of contrasting air.

alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep grey beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
caption: Siccar Point: Devonian sandstone overlies much older, tilted Silurian beds. The unconformity records deformation, erosion and missing time.

alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
caption: Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Flowing ice carries debris; its dark medial moraines record where tributary glaciers join.

alt: A physical marker of the historic Greenwich Meridian at the Royal Observatory.
caption: The historic Greenwich Meridian makes a reference longitude tangible. Modern WGS84 zero longitude lies about 102 metres east of this line.

alt: USGS topographic map extract showing Yosemite Creek, a campground, contours and coordinate markings.
caption: A real USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Read the sheet's coordinate system and scale before giving a position; it is not an OS National Grid map.

alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
caption: USGS gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica, 12 December 2001. Repeated measurements of stage and discharge produce a river's hydrograph.

credit: Colin Smith / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: People cross pale limestone blocks separated by deep joints above Malham Cove, England.
caption: Malham Cove limestone pavement. Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide widens joints into grykes, leaving blocks called clints.

credit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Layered cliffs, mesas and deeply incised valleys of the Grand Canyon in evening light.
caption: Grand Canyon from Hopi Point, Arizona. Resistant beds form steps and cliffs above valleys cut by running water.

credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

alt: A thin sunlit lunar crescent with crater shadows along the terminator against black space.
caption: The Artemis II crew photographed this lunar crescent on 7 April 2026. Phase is the visible fraction of the sunlit hemisphere, not Earth's shadow.

alt: False-colour MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
caption: MODIS, 2 May 2001: thermal contrast traces the Gulf Stream and eddies. Brightness temperature includes the sea surface and overlying moist atmosphere.

alt: Polygonal ground and ponds on the tundra in Noatak National Preserve, Alaska, photographed from the air.
caption: Ice-wedge polygons in Alaska's Noatak tundra. Repeated thermal contraction cracking and ice growth organise the permafrost landscape.

credit: Olga Ernst / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Steep dark rock walls border the Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland.
caption: Almannagjá, Þingvellir: faults accommodate extension within Iceland's broad North American–Eurasian plate boundary zone.

credit: none (Landsat) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: False-colour Landsat image of the Lena Delta with many branching distributaries and islands.
caption: Landsat's view of the Lena Delta, 2000. Distributaries spread sediment into the Arctic Ocean. The image combines infrared and red bands.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Sediment circulating in eddies abrades the bedrock, enlarging these potholes.

credit: Walter Siegmund / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: Floodwater from the Stillaguamish River surrounds a picnic table and trees.
caption: The South Fork Stillaguamish River in flood. Water spreads beyond the usual channel when discharge exceeds channel capacity.

credit: NASA/Kjell Lindgren / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Ucayali River, Peru, photographed from the ISS. Meander migration leaves cut-offs and abandoned channels across the floodplain.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: South African city lights beneath a curved glowing atmospheric horizon and stars, viewed from the ISS.
caption: South Africa on Earth's night side, seen from the ISS. Rotation carries locations through sunlight and darkness; this is a photograph of the night hemisphere.

credit: National Oceanic & Atmospheric Adminstration (NOAA) / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Rounded pillow lava on a fissured seafloor at the Galápagos Rift, photographed by a NOAA expedition.
caption: NOAA, Galápagos Rift, 21 July 2011. Lava quenched in seawater forms pillows close to a spreading centre, where new oceanic crust is built.

credit: NASA/Apollo 17 crew; taken by either Harrison Schmitt or Ron Evans / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The fully sunlit Earth showing Africa, Arabia, Antarctica and swirling clouds in the Apollo 17 photograph.
caption: Apollo 17's Blue Marble, 7 December 1972. Earth's axial tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight over the year.

credit: Willem van Aken, CSIRO / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
alt: Bare eroded soil with small gullies on a hillslope near Charters Towers, Queensland.
caption: Hillslope gully and sheet erosion near Charters Towers, Queensland, documented by CSIRO. Loss of cover exposes soil to runoff.

credit: NPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: National Park Service soil scientists examine a freshly sampled soil profile and record its texture.
caption: NPS fieldwork at Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park. Texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral soil.

alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.
caption: A working sundial at Green's Windmill, Nottingham. A gnomon's shadow connects the Sun's apparent direction with local solar time.

credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-colour mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

credit: NOAA Photo Library / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of damaged buildings and washed-over land on the Bolivar Peninsula after Hurricane Ike.
caption: Bolivar Peninsula, Texas, September 2008. NOAA documented coastal damage from Hurricane Ike's storm surge.

alt: Extreme-ultraviolet observation of the full Sun showing bright active regions, displayed in yellow.
caption: SDO's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly, 18 December 2015. This false-colour ultraviolet observation reveals the hot solar atmosphere, not the Sun's visible colour.

credit: Jesse Allen, NASA Earth Observatory, using data obtained from the Goddard Earth Sciences DAAC. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Parallel rows of clouds extend from sea ice across open water in the Bering Sea.
caption: Cloud streets over the Bering Sea, 20 January 2006. Cold air over warmer water supports convection organised into rolls by the wind.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: GOES-East satellite view of the Americas with tropical cloud bands and midlatitude weather systems.
caption: GOES-East, 22 April 2014 at 11:45 UTC. Cloud belts reveal aspects of global circulation; a single image does not outline every atmospheric cell.

credit: Dennis G. Jarvis / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A fishing boat rests on exposed mud beside a wharf at low tide in Nova Scotia.
caption: Low tide at Waterford on St Mary's Bay, Nova Scotia. The exposed harbour floor makes tidal range visible.

alt: The clear eye and tall spiral cloud walls of Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the ISS.
caption: Astronaut Ed Lu photographed Hurricane Isabel on 13 September 2003. The eye is surrounded by the eyewall's deep convective clouds.

alt: Debris, damaged buildings and inundated land at a fishing port near Kesennuma after the 2011 tsunami.
caption: Kesennuma, Japan, after the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. This aerial photograph records inundation damage; it does not show a breaking tsunami wave.

alt: A Hubble mosaic of Andromeda's bright central region, dark dust lanes and densely packed stars.
caption: NASA/ESA Hubble mosaic of Andromeda. Resolved stars and dust lanes provide an observed view of a galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away.

caption: Kīlauea, 25 February 1983. USGS photographed a lava fountain approximately 10 metres high; molten rock is at the surface, not throughout the mantle.

alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
caption: Evaporation fog over a lake. Water vapour mixes into colder air and condenses into droplets; invisible vapour itself cannot be photographed.

alt: Rounded remnants of granite emerge from loose weathered material in an exposed rock profile.
caption: Weathered granite documented by GeoDIL. Mineral breakdown and disintegration progressively turn intact rock into weathered material.

alt: Long fault-bounded valleys and escarpments in Kenya's East African Rift, viewed from the ISS.
caption: The East African Rift in Kenya: continental extension is an opening stage of a possible ocean-basin cycle. A rift does not inevitably become an ocean.

alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organise minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

caption: A measured field profile in Wuhlheide, Berlin. Colour and texture vary down the soil; horizon boundaries must be identified from field evidence.

caption: A windsock responds to moving air. Its open mouth faces into the wind; meteorological wind direction names where the air comes from.

alt: A low grassy coastal terrace below an older cliff near Northbank.
caption: A raised beach near Northbank. Former shorelines record changes in relative sea level, which can include land uplift after unloading of ice.

alt: Hawaiian islands with greener windward slopes, drier leeward slopes and silvery sunglint on the Pacific.
caption: Terra MODIS, 27 May 2003. Northeasterly trade winds favour wetter, greener windward slopes; leeward slopes are drier. The bright ocean is sunglint.

alt: A karst spring in Alabama flows over rocks from a wooded limestone slope.
caption: Groundwater emerges at a karst spring in Alabama. Water stored in connected pores and fractures can return to the surface as spring flow.

alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

alt: Circular plates of new pancake ice cover the surface of the western Ross Sea in Antarctica.
caption: New sea ice forming in the Ross Sea. Freezing rejects much of the salt into the surrounding water, increasing its density and helping drive polar overturning.

credit: USGS Office of Groundwater / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS map showing the distribution of principal aquifers across the United States.
caption: USGS principal aquifers of the United States, 2000. Colours identify aquifer systems; the map does not show water-table depth or whether a particular well is confined.

alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

alt: Fossilised Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
caption: Ogyopsis klotzi from the Middle Cambrian Mount Stephen Trilobite Beds, Canada. Fossils help correlate and interpret ancient sedimentary rocks.

alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
caption: Glacial terrain in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. Ice erosion enlarges mountain hollows into cirques and sharpens the ridges between them.

alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
caption: Kaolinite from Ixtassou, France, is a clay mineral. Clay as a soil texture means particles smaller than 0.002 mm; mineral identity and particle size are different properties.

alt: The Moselle joins the wider Rhine beside the city of Koblenz, Germany.
caption: The Rhine–Moselle confluence at Koblenz, photographed in 1988. A tributary joins the main channel here.

Mike Doukas, USGS

alt: Deep blue Crater Lake fills a broad volcanic depression, with Wizard Island near its western shore.
caption: USGS aerial photograph of Crater Lake, Oregon. Collapse following the eruption of Mount Mazama formed the caldera; Wizard Island is a younger volcanic cone.

alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

alt: Landsat view of the Thames estuary, coastal shallows and offshore wind farms.
caption: NASA Landsat observation of the Thames estuary. The tidal river widens towards the North Sea; pale water reveals suspended material and shallow coastal water.

alt: Fallen leaves and organic litter beneath white beech trees in New South Wales, Australia.
caption: White beech leaf litter at Carowiry Creek, New South Wales. Organic material on the forest floor stores carbon and provides material for decomposition.

credit: Edal Anton Lefterov / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Brown coal exposed at Chukurovo in Bulgaria.
caption: Lignite at Chukurovo, Bulgaria. This fossil fuel formed from buried plant material; combustion transfers its stored carbon to the atmosphere.

credit: Rémih / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: A bank of cloud spills over a mountain ridge above Cilaos on Réunion.
caption: A föhn cloud wall above Cilaos, Réunion. Moist air rises on the windward side; descending air on the lee side warms as it is compressed.

credit: Doc Searls from Santa Barbara, USA / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Aerial view of elongated low hills around Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin.
caption: Drumlin terrain near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin. The streamlined hills record former glacier flow; they are landforms left after the ice retreated.

credit: Iraphne R. Childs / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
caption: Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, in the 1980s. A groyne interrupts sediment movement along a beach and can change sediment supply farther down-drift.

credit: Eric Jones / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Crearlagh Burn descends from a higher tributary valley towards a deeper main valley.
caption: The hanging valley of Crearlagh Burn, Scotland. Tributary valleys can be left above a main trough when a larger glacier erodes more deeply.

credit: GlacierNPS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The sharp summit and steep ridges of Little Matterhorn in Glacier National Park, Montana.
caption: Little Matterhorn, Glacier National Park, USA. Glacial erosion on several sides can leave a sharp pyramidal peak; this is not the Matterhorn in the Alps.

credit: Colin Kinnear / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Cloud lies below the summit of Cruach Ardrain in Scotland.
caption: Low cloud beneath Cruach Ardrain. A temperature inversion can trap cool, moist air below warmer air; a photograph alone cannot measure the temperature profile.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: NickLongrich / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Exposed layers of the Scollard Formation beside the Red Deer River in Alberta.
caption: The K–Pg boundary in the Scollard Formation, Alberta, Canada. The rock record preserves evidence of the transition around 66 million years ago.

credit: Jocelyn Augustino / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A raised embankment separates floodwater from farmland beside the Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri.
caption: Mississippi levee at Hannibal, Missouri, 20 June 2008. This engineered embankment limits inundation; natural levees instead build up from repeated overbank deposition.

credit: Chris M Morris / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A mesquite shrub grows on a mound of trapped sand in the Mojave Desert.
caption: Mesquite in Mojave National Preserve, California. Vegetation traps wind-blown sand and can build a small dune called a nabkha.

credit: NASA/JHUAPL / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: MESSENGER global mosaic of Mercury showing its cratered surface.
caption: NASA MESSENGER mosaic of Mercury, 2011. Spacecraft observations reveal the planet's cratered rocky surface; this is a composite, not a single exposure.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer; pumping may lower the water level around a well, which is measured below ground.

credit: USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Pale pyroclastic deposits fill the Marella River valley below Mount Pinatubo.
caption: USGS photograph of Pinatubo's Marella River valley, 1 July 1991. These are deposits left by pyroclastic flows, not a view of a flow in motion.

credit: Paul Wynter / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Graw DFM radiosondes and a radio receiver arranged on a table.
caption: Balloon-borne radiosondes transmit measurements of the atmosphere. Profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure help locate inversions and estimate lapse rates.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: A reverse fault offsets contrasting mineral layers in a rock sample from the Stillwater Complex, Montana.
caption: Reverse fault in layered igneous rock from Montana's Stillwater Complex. Trace matching layers across the break: the hanging wall moved up relative to the footwall.

credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

credit: Jakub Hałun / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: The isolated rock stack Hvítserkur rises from shallow coastal water in northwestern Iceland.
caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland. This isolated coastal rock illustrates a stack, with openings cut through its base.

credit: Thomas Pratt, USGS. Public domain. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS scientists install a field seismometer at Sabana Yeguas, Puerto Rico.
caption: USGS seismometer installation at Sabana Yeguas, Puerto Rico, 10 January 2020. Recorded ground motion distinguishes P, S and surface-wave arrivals; the photograph shows the measuring instrument.

credit: Daredeep33 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Turquoise water fills the steep-sided Bimmah sinkhole in Oman.
caption: Bimmah sinkhole, Oman. Dissolution and collapse in soluble rock can create closed depressions called dolines.

credit: USFS employees / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Melting snow patches and a stream near Fourth of July Lake in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains.
caption: Snowmelt near Fourth of July Lake, Idaho. Seasonal melting transfers stored snow water into streams, soils and groundwater.

credit: Plorpy2 / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Photographs of clay samples comparing grey reduced material and oxidised reddish material.
caption: Real clay samples showing contrasting redox conditions. Prolonged saturation restricts oxygen, often producing grey gley colours; oxidation can produce reddish mottles.

credit: The original uploader was Michaila vnuk at Ukrainian Wikipedia. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A soil profile on the Karelian Isthmus with a dark surface, pale leached layer and browner subsoil.
caption: Podzolic soil on the Karelian Isthmus. The pale E horizon has lost material by eluviation; material may accumulate in the B horizon below.

credit: Zde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Calcite stalactites hang from the roof of a cave on Mount Kyllini, Greece.
caption: Stalactites in a cave on Mount Kyllini. Dissolved calcium carbonate is deposited as water drips and loses carbon dioxide.

credit: Explorer2310 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: Microscope photograph of leaf epidermal cells and stomatal pores under drought conditions.
caption: Leaf epidermis viewed through a microscope. Stomata regulate gas exchange and water-vapour loss; transpiration is one part of evapotranspiration.

credit: Midori / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0 · resized
alt: The broad conical slopes of Mount Fuji rise beyond Lake Kawaguchi in Japan.
caption: Mount Fuji from Lake Kawaguchi, Japan. Repeated eruptions built a stratovolcano with layers of lava and fragmental deposits.

credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center from Greenbelt, MD, USA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An SDO observation of the solar photosphere showing a large dark sunspot group.
caption: NASA SDO observation of active region AR 12192 in 2014. Sunspots are cooler areas of the photosphere; the orange display colour is image processing.

credit: David Medcalf / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: An exposed bank of poorly sorted glacial sediment containing stones of several sizes.
caption: A natural exposure of glacial till. Ice deposits a mixture of grain sizes directly, often without the sorting produced by flowing water.

credit: Yyuri1989 / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized

alt: Grey London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
caption: London Clay forms the lower part of the Naze cliffs. Clay-rich beds commonly transmit groundwater slowly and can act as aquitards; the cliff exposes the material, while permeability is established by testing.

alt: A broad, grassy former river valley near Blumberg, now drained by the much smaller Aitrach.
caption: The Aitrach valley preserves the former route of the Feldberg Danube. Capture by the Wutach diverted its large upstream flow towards the Rhine, leaving the small Aitrach in an oversized valley. The channel itself is difficult to distinguish in this landscape view.
